working: Substitute \(u = 1-x\) (King's reflection on [0,1]): \(\int_0^1 x(1-x)^{-3/4}dx = \int_0^1 (1-u)u^{-3/4}du = \int_0^1 (u^{-3/4} - u^{1/4})du = 4 - \frac{4}{5} = \frac{16}{5}\). Numerically confirmed via the smoothing substitution \(x = 1-t^4\), which gives \(\int_0^1 4(1-t^4)dt = 3.2000\) exactly.

working: R = {(x,y) in N^2 : 2x+y=41}. Not reflexive: 3x=41 has no natural solution. Not symmetric: (1,39) is in R (2+39=41) but (39,1) is not (78+1=79). Not transitive: (11,19) is in R (22+19=41) and (19,3) is in R (38+3=41), but (11,3) gives 22+3=25 != 41. Hence none of the three properties holds.

working: Write \(v = (p,q,r)^T\); then \(B = vv^T\) and \(A\) is the skew-symmetric cross-product matrix for \(v\), so \(Av = v \times v = 0\). Hence \(AB = (Av)v^T = 0\), the null matrix. Verified numerically with \(p=2, q=-3, r=5\): every entry of AB is 0.

working: For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&a\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), induction gives \(A^n = \begin{bmatrix}1&na\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\), so \(A^4 = \begin{bmatrix}1&4a\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Checked numerically with \(a=7\): \(A^4 = \begin{bmatrix}1&28\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(28 = 4\times 7\).

working: With \(A^T = A\) and \(B^T = B\): \((AB-BA)^T = (AB)^T-(BA)^T = B^TA^T - A^TB^T = BA - AB = -(AB-BA)\). A matrix equal to the negative of its transpose is skew-symmetric. It need not be null, since AB and BA generally differ.

working: For an n x n matrix, scaling every entry by k scales the determinant by \(k^n\) (k factors out of each of the n rows). So \(|A| = |kB| = k^n|B|\). Verified numerically for n=3 with k=2.5: \(|kB|/|B| = 15.625 = 2.5^3\).

working: \(A+B\) defined forces A and B to have the same order, say m x n. \(AB\) defined then forces columns of A = rows of B, i.e. n = m. So both are square matrices of the same order. (C) is a true but incomplete consequence; (B) is the full conclusion.

working: Left-multiply \(B = -A^{-1}BA\) by A: \(AB = -BA\), i.e. \(AB+BA = 0\). Then \((A+B)^2 = A^2 + AB + BA + B^2 = A^2 + B^2\). Verified with \(A = \mathrm{diag}(1,-1)\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\), which satisfy the hypothesis: \((A+B)^2 = 2I = A^2+B^2\), and it is not the zero matrix, so (A) is wrong.

working: \(A^2 = A\cdot A = (AB)A = A(BA) = AB = A\) and \(B^2 = B\cdot B = (BA)B = B(AB) = BA = B\), so both are idempotent. Verified with the genuine pair \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (A != B, AB=A, BA=B, both idempotent).

working: Let \(f(x) = \cos x - x + \tfrac{1}{2}\). Then \(f(0) = 1.5 > 0\) and \(f(\pi/2) = -1.0708 < 0\), so by the Intermediate Value Theorem a root lies in \([0,\pi/2]\). The other intervals show no sign change: \(f(-\pi/2) = 2.0708\) and \(f(0) = 1.5\) (both positive); \(f\) is negative throughout \([\pi/2,\pi]\) and \([\pi,3\pi/2]\). Also \(f'(x) = -\sin x - 1 \le 0\), so the root is unique.
subtopic: General Solutions and Counting Solutions of Trigonometric Equations
